questions.q: Define "non-SNA production work" in the context of household management and give two examples from a typical Indian household.
questions.a: Non-SNA production work refers to unpaid activities that produce goods or services for own-consumption within the household and are not counted in the System of National Accounts (GDP). Examples: cooking meals for the family, caring for children/elderly, cleaning, fetching water, managing household finances. A wrong answer (e.g., "work done by a maid" or "paid tutoring") reveals confusion between market/paid work and unpaid household production, and ignorance of the SNA boundary — a critical error in board questions on valuation of women's work.

questions.q: Explain why the "replacement cost method" of valuing a homemaker's work may overestimate or underestimate its true economic value. Use the concept of "specialised household capital" in your answer.
questions.a: Replacement cost sums market wages for each task (cook, cleaner, nurse, driver, tutor) but ignores that a homemaker develops specialised household capital — context-specific knowledge (family dietary needs, medical history, school schedules, financial priorities) that a market substitute lacks, leading to underestimation of efficiency and quality. Conversely, it overestimates if market rates include overheads (agency fees, profit margins) not incurred at home. A wrong answer focusing only on "market wages are higher/lower" misses the human-capital dimension tested in CBSE case-based questions.

questions.q: A family of four (two working parents, two school-going children) decides to redistribute household tasks. The mother currently spends 4 hours/day on cooking/cleaning, father 0.5 hours, children 0.5 hours combined. They agree each adult should contribute 2 hours/day and children 30 minutes/day. Calculate the time transfer required from mother to father, and propose two specific tasks the father could take over that leverage his existing skills (e.g., financial management, digital literacy).
questions.a: Mother's current: 4 hrs; target: 2 hrs → reduction of 2 hrs (120 min). Father's current: 0.5 hrs; target: 2 hrs → increase of 1.5 hrs (90 min). Children: current 0.5 hrs → target 0.5 hrs (no change). Time transfer from mother to father = 90 min (father's deficit); remaining 30 min absorbed by efficiency gains/outsourcing. Tasks for father: (1) Monthly budgeting, bill payments, investment tracking — leverages financial literacy; (2) Online grocery ordering, school fee portals, medical appointment scheduling — leverages digital literacy. A wrong answer that suggests "father cooks dinner" without skill-matching ignores the competency-based allocation principle central to Class 12 resource management.

questions.q: Compare the "gender-essentialist" and "time-availability" models of household labour division. Which model better explains the persistence of unequal division in dual-earner Indian middle-class households? Justify with two pieces of evidence from time-use surveys (e.g., NSSO 2019).
questions.a: Gender-essentialist model: division based on innate gender roles (women = nurturers, men = providers). Time-availability model: division based on relative hours in paid work. NSSO 2019 shows: (1) Employed women spend 299 min/day on unpaid domestic work vs. 97 min for employed men — a 3:1 gap despite similar paid-work hours; (2) Unemployed men still do less domestic work (125 min) than employed women (299 min). Time-availability model fails; gender norms persist. A wrong answer citing "women work fewer paid hours" misreads the data and misses the structural gender bias — a frequent board exam trap.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "Introducing paternity leave alone will achieve shared responsibility in Indian households." Evaluate using the concepts of social norms, workplace culture, and economic opportunity cost.
questions.a: Paternity leave is necessary but insufficient. Social norms: "good father = provider" discourages leave uptake (India's paternity leave uptake <5% where available). Workplace culture: stigma, career penalties, lack of replacement staff. Economic opportunity cost: men's higher average wages make their leave costlier for families. True sharing requires: (1) non-transferable "use-it-or-lose-it" quotas (Nordic model), (2) subsidised childcare, (3) flexible work for all, (4) school/community programmes normalising male caregiving. A wrong answer treating policy as a silver bullet ignores implementation gaps and cultural embeddedness — a key evaluation skill for competency questions.

questions.q: Design a "Household Responsibility Charter" template for a three-generation family (grandparents, parents, two adolescents) that operationalises shared responsibility. Include: task categories, negotiation principles, review mechanism, and a method to value invisible cognitive labour (planning, worrying, remembering).
questions.a: Template: (1) Categories: Daily care (meals, hygiene, meds), Maintenance (cleaning, repairs, bills), Cognitive/Managerial (scheduling, inventory, school/health coordination), Emotional (listening, conflict mediation, festival planning). (2) Negotiation: weekly 30-min meeting; tasks assigned by skill/interest/time, not age/gender; "swap clause" for burnout. (3) Review: monthly "audit" using time-use logs; adjust for exams, illness, festivals. (4) Valuing cognitive labour: assign "mental load points" (1-5) per task; total points distributed equally; points convert to leisure-time credits or budget allocation. A poor answer lists chores only, omitting cognitive/emotional labour and review mechanism — missing the management-process lens (planning, controlling) central to this chapter.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The role of homemaker refers to the ______ responsibility of managing a household's human, material, and financial resources to ensure the well-being and development of all family members; changing perspectives recognise this as skilled, economic labour requiring shared responsibility across gender and generational lines rather than the sole duty of one individual.

Fill in the blank: Imagine a Class 12 student, Priya, observing her mother manage the household while working full-time — cooking, budgeting, ______ repairs, caring for grandparents, and helping with homework — while her father contributes financially but rarely participates in daily chores.
Fill in the blank: What would a fair division look like?" Start by mapping a typical day's activities for each family member using a ______-hour time-use diary.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
